**www.woodmac.com** Between a rock and a hard place?
The future of taxation in the mining sector
**Return to the Global Horizons Service** **Delivering commercial insight** **www.woodmac.com** # **Exec Summary** Over the past decade, petroleum prices and company profits have soared. This escalation in prices and profits, along with challenging economic conditions, drove governments to a wave of new ‘resource nationalism’ policies – from outright nationalisation of companies in some extreme cases, to more typical increases in protectionism and/or government take from taxes/royalties, ownership restructuring, and contract revisions. Mining companies have averaged much better to-date, but the sector is under increasing pressure. Many governments are looking to increase their revenues from the industry– from current demands in South Africa for mining to contribute ‘its fair share,’ policy changes in many South American countries, on to Australia’s new MRRT tax to name a few. With a subdued price outlook, 2013 could be an opportunity window for mining companies to collaborate with governments on future terms – or risk potential confrontation in the longer-term and further erode their margins. In this presentation, we look at parallels between mining and petroleum so as to assess what the mining sector can anticipate in this shifting price environment. **© Wood Mackenzie 2** **Delivering commercial insight** **www.woodmac.com** **Petroleum prices and company profits have soared over the past decade… driving governments to an upsurge in new ‘resource nationalism’ policies** 100

Ni, Bx, Fe, C|2|The gold rush began in 1850 near New South Wales, which lasted decades before taking the country into a recession.
Today Australia is a diversified economy but remains one of the top producers of gold, copper, zinc, nickel, iron ore,
coal and bauxite. The Mineral Resource Rent Tax (MRRT) came into effect in July 2012; it was originally drafted to
apply to the entire mining sector but revised to target only the coal and iron ore industries (when profits are over $75m)
currently controlled by the international mining giants Anglo American, BHP Billiton, Rio Tinto and Xstrata. The
government has also intervened in acquisitions by Chinese entities.| |Indonesia|Au, Cu, Ni,

, iron and steel is controlled by a handful of state-owned companies. The
government also holds equity interests in Freeport’s Grasberg mine and Newmont’s Batu Hijau mine which account for
the country’s copper and gold production. The 2009 mining law included among other things royalties and a 10% Net
Profit Payment. In 2010, Indonesia agreed to implement a 2-year ban on permits for forest clearing in relation to
Norway’s $2Bn climate aid deal. In 2011, the government passed a new regulation requiring coal producers to sell a
minimum 24% of production to the domestic market. Indonesia’s mining policy will continue to evolve with a focus on
maximising national consumption of domestic production, and potentially an increased state involvement to further

part of a larger infrastructure deal. In 2012, the country was negotiating a similar deal with Japan.| |Chile|Cu||2|The current mining code allows any individual or company to participate in exploration and development; also, the tax
invariability law applies to foreign investors who are required to pay a combined tax rate of 42%. In 2006, a sliding-
scale royalty based on copper production was introduced ranging from 0% to 5%. In 2010, the rates were increased to
between 4% and 9% to assist earthquake reconstruction projects. Rates were expected to return to 4%-5% between
2013 and 2017. The mining industry contributes a significant proportion of the country’s GDP, foreign exports and
government revenues, and the State holds a considerable interest in mining through CODELCO. Given that income
inequality is high and elections are to be held in 2013, political parties may feel popular pressure to increase and
redistribute the economic contributions of mining to the country.| © Wood Mackenzie 10 **Delivering commercial insight** **www.woodmac.com** ## **The mining community responds to the risk of policy changes** #### **_Confrontation?_** #### **_Cooperation?_** - **Trusting in lobbying / negotiators to keep government take as low as possible for as long as possible, noting a subdued price outlook for some commodities and softening of company profits in the near-term** - **Deferring/delaying projects in high risk countries, and shifting investment to countries offering better terms** - **Negotiating value trade-offs with less politically sensitive policies than resource nationalism** - **Fostering a greater understanding of the value a mining project brings to the host government** - **Ensuring governments are sufficiently educated about the risks and investment decision-making processes in the business – and are realistic about the resource potential** - **Better communicating the implications of changes in the risk/reward equation, that preserve the value to both the companies and the governments** - **Warning governments that investment could dry up if taxes or other means of government take increase** **Delivering commercial insight** **© Wood Mackenzie 11** **www.woodmac.com** ## **Moving forward, a bearish price forecast in commodities may help ease the pressure on the extractive sector** #### **Growth in Petroleum & Minerals Prices 2003-2014** 900

**There are a few countries where mining accounts for a small part of the overall economy or where governments are attempting to

encourage the industry:** **Greece/Portugal** - As a result of the financial crisis, southern European countries are “fast-tracking” mining licenses and adopting policies to encourage mining FDI. Governments need to generate employment and receive fresh cash. **And in a lower-price environment in the coming years, governments may gradually lower their demands on the mining industry. However, we still expect some mining policy changes in parts of the world in 2013. Some of the countries to watch are:** **Chile –** 2013 presidential elections may be a crucial moment to open debate on contribution of copper to the national economy. **Mongolia** – Government continues to suggest it wants a majority stake in the Oyu Tolgoi copper mine. **China** – Government adopted more stringent environmental regulations and announced it will close 5,000 non-coal mines in 2013.
